title: Eight Weeks of Not Carrying It Alone
subtitle: An eight week plan from James Bell for the one caring for an aging parent or a sick spouse. Honest about the guilt and the grief, practical about help and rest, and clear that no one can carry this alone.
intro:
This is an eight week plan for the one caring for an aging parent, or for a husband or wife, while the caring wears you down. Each week holds one focus, one small daily practice, one thing to read, one tool to use, and one honest question, and every practice is small enough for a bad day, because many of your days may be bad ones right now. It moves slowly on purpose, from naming what the care is costing you and the guilt that comes with it, through asking for specific help, arranging real rest, and tending your own body, down to the harder ground underneath: grief for someone who is still alive, honor toward a parent who was hard to love, and the decisions about care. It ends with a life you can keep through these years and after them. Nothing in it will make your parent well. It's meant to keep you from carrying this alone.

It isn't a cure, and it isn't a substitute for a doctor, a licensed counselor, a pastor, or the real people who can take a shift, and nothing here is legal or financial advice. If you're afraid you might hurt your parent, call or text 988 today, before anything else on this page; you don't have to be suicidal to call. If someone is hurting, neglecting, or taking money from your parent, report it to adult protective services, and call 911 if anyone is in danger. Walk the plan imperfectly. A missed week is not failure; you just pick it back up, and some weeks the question will be all you can manage. That counts.
careNote: If you've stopped sleeping or eating, can't stop crying, or feel resentment hardening into rage, see your own doctor and a licensed counselor and tell them you're a caregiver. In a crisis, call or text 988; if someone is harming your parent, report it to adult protective services, and if anyone is in danger, call 911.

weeks.focus: Naming the cost and the guilt
weeks.why: Caregiving rarely arrives all at once. It grows from a fall or a diagnosis into appointments and pill organizers, calls in the night, and a life of your own that has quietly thinned out. Under the tiredness there are usually things you haven't said aloud: resentment toward your parent for needing so much and toward others for helping so little, then guilt for resenting people you love, and sometimes a wish that it were all over, which you were ashamed to have thought. None of that cancels your love. It means you're carrying more than one person was made to carry. Paul didn't hide his limits from the Corinthians; he told them he and his companions had been "under a burden far beyond our ability to endure" (2 Corinthians 1:8). A weight you won't name can't be shared.
weeks.practice: Each night, write two plain sentences: what the care took from you today, and one feeling about it you haven't said aloud, resentment included. On the worst nights one sentence will do. Before the week ends, tell one person the whole truth about how you're doing. If you're afraid of losing control with your parent, or your thoughts turn toward ending your own life, don't wait: make sure everyone is safe, tell someone today, and call or text 988.

read.label: How to Face Your Own Limits Without Despair, on the guilt of never being enough for everyone

tool.label: The Emotional Health Self-Check, fifteen questions on rest, grief, and boundaries, a mirror and not a diagnosis

weeks.reflection: What has this care cost me that I haven't let myself say out loud, and who taught me that saying it would mean I don't love them?

weeks.why: When Moses sat alone settling Israel's disputes from morning until evening, his father-in-law Jethro watched for a day and then told him the truth: "What you are doing is not good. Surely you and these people with you will wear yourselves out, because the task is too heavy for you. You cannot handle it alone" (Exodus 18:17-18). The work needed many hands, and Moses had two. Most of us absorbed a picture of the good life as independent, where needing help means you've failed, and the church has often preached honor as if it meant doing everything yourself. I'm a pastor, and that failure is mine too. In practice, help tends to come when one person is asked for one thing at a set time, and rarely from a vague offer to help sometime.
weeks.practice: Each day this week, add to one list whatever the care took that day: the rides, the pills, the calls, the paperwork, the nights. Each day, pray by name for one person who might help. Before the week ends, ask one of them for one specific thing, with a day and a time, like sitting with your father on Thursday afternoon. If they say no, it isn't a verdict on you; ask someone else next week.

read.label: Exodus 18 in the Study Bible, where Jethro tells Moses the work is too heavy to do alone

tool.label: The Prayer Planner, give each person you might ask a day of the week in your prayers

weeks.reflection: Who has offered to help that I've never actually asked, and what am I afraid it would say about me if I did?

weeks.why: Mark's Gospel tells of a day so crowded that the disciples "did not even have time to eat." Jesus said to them, "Come with Me privately to a solitary place, and let us rest for a while" (Mark 6:31). The rest was his idea. Then the crowd ran ahead and was waiting on the shore, and he taught them instead (Mark 6:33-34). Rest rarely goes to plan for caregivers either, which is a reason to arrange it on purpose rather than wait for a quiet week that never comes. Respite care exists for this: a helper at the house for a few hours, an adult day program, a short stay in a care facility. An afternoon away is part of the care, because a caregiver who never rests eventually has nothing left to give.
weeks.practice: This week, make one call about respite, to your parent's doctor's office, a social worker, or the agency on aging that serves your parent's area, and ask what help exists so you can rest; if your parent is on hospice, ask the hospice team. Put one break on the calendar, even an hour, and guard it. Each day, take ten minutes that belong to no one else, outside if you can.

read.label: How to Receive Rest as a Gift, Not a Reward, for the guilt that says you haven't earned a break

tool.label: Mark 6 in the Study Bible, where Jesus calls his tired disciples away to rest

weeks.reflection: What do I fear will happen if I step away for an afternoon, and what is never stepping away already costing both of us?

weeks.why: Caregivers tend to keep everyone's appointments but their own. You may know your mother's medications by heart and not remember your last checkup, and you may lie awake listening for footsteps in the hall. The body you're spending is the one you'll still live in when this season ends. A psalm that bears David's name says of God, "For He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust" (Psalm 103:14). He remembers what you're made of on the days you forget it, and tending your own body is part of how the care keeps going. If you've been drinking more to get through the evenings, tell a doctor; after heavy drinking, stopping suddenly can be dangerous, and the Find Help page lists SAMHSA's helpline.
weeks.practice: Each day, do one plain mercy for your own body: a real meal, a glass of water, a ten minute walk, or going to bed when your parent does. One is enough. This week, call your own doctor, make an appointment, and say you're a caregiver. If your nights are broken, ask one person to take one night so you can sleep through it.

read.label: How to Steward Your Health, on why tending your own body isn't self-absorption

tool.label: The Worry Journal, five minutes before bed to set down what isn't yours to carry tonight

weeks.reflection: When did I last care for my own body the way I care for theirs, and what would I tell a friend in my place?

weeks.why: Some of what wears you out is grief. If your parent has dementia or a long decline, you may be losing them in pieces too small for anyone else to notice. The family therapist Pauline Boss named this ambiguous loss: someone present in body and slipping away in mind. There's no funeral and no casseroles, so no one thinks to comfort you, and you may not think you're allowed to grieve. You are. In the book of Isaiah, Zion complains that the Lord has forgotten her, and God answers by imagining the unthinkable, a mother forgetting her child: "Even if she could forget, I will not forget you!" (Isaiah 49:15). God's memory was never as fragile as ours, and you're allowed to miss them while they're still in the room.
weeks.practice: Each day, write down one specific thing you miss about your parent as they were, the way he told a story or the way she said your name, and tell it to God as a loss. Once this week, pray Psalm 13 slowly; it bears David's name and asks whether God has forgotten him. When you visit, let go of needing to be recognized. Hold a hand, sing a song they still know, and let the hour count even if it's gone from their mind by supper.

read.label: How Do You Honor Aging Parents Who Need Care? Its opening names the long goodbye, grief for someone still alive

tool.label: Isaiah 49 in the Study Bible, where God answers a people who feel forgotten

weeks.reflection: What have I already lost of the parent I knew, and have I let anyone, God included, comfort me for it?

weeks.focus: Honoring a parent who was hard
weeks.why: For some caregivers the hardest part is older than the illness. If the parent you're caring for was harsh, absent, or cruel, the care lands on an old wound, and "Honor your father and mother" (Exodus 20:12) can sound like a demand to forget it. The Hebrew word for honor comes from a root meaning heavy; to honor someone is to treat them as weighty, a person who still counts. We in the church have sometimes swung this command like a whip, but it has never required obedience to harm, trust that wasn't earned, or pretending the past didn't happen, and forgiving someone isn't the same as making yourself available to them. Some adult children give care with firm limits; others honor a parent by arranging care through other hands and checking on it from a distance. A counselor who understands abuse can help you see which is wise.
weeks.practice: Each day, write one honest sentence about what this parent did or failed to do, and one about what you can give now without putting yourself within reach of harm. Choose one limit that makes the care survivable, a shorter visit or a helper in the room, and keep it. If you're afraid of them, parent or spouse, get safe first: call 911 in danger, and the National Domestic Violence Hotline, listed on Find Help, can help you plan.

read.label: How to Love a Difficult Family Member, on honor that is neither obedience nor a surrender of your safety

tool.label: The Find Help page, where the National Domestic Violence Hotline is listed with the other help lines

weeks.reflection: What can I honestly give this parent without stepping back within reach of harm, and who could help me see that line clearly?

weeks.why: Sooner or later come the decisions: who will do what, who will pay for what, where your parent will live, and which papers need signing while your parent can still understand them. Whether honor leans toward keeping a parent at home as long as it can be safely done, or can be given through other hands in a good facility you choose and visit faithfully, is a question faithful Christians answer differently. The care page sets out both views and lands on neither, and neither will this plan. Both agree that abandonment is never honor and that safety comes first. As he was dying, Jesus couldn't take his mother home himself, so he gave her into the keeping of the disciple he loved (John 19:26-27). Arranging care through other hands is different from walking away.
weeks.practice: Each day, pray one sentence asking for wisdom about the next decision, not all of them. This week, make one call that opens a door: set a family meeting, ask your parent's doctor for a social worker, or ask an elder law attorney about a durable power of attorney and a health care proxy. This isn't legal or financial advice. If anyone is hurting or neglecting your parent, at home or in a facility, report it to adult protective services.

read.label: Caring for my parent is wearing me out: the care page, with the nursing home question weighed both ways and the calls that open doors

tool.label: The Prayer Generator, with a prayer to pray before a hard conversation

weeks.reflection: What decision have I been putting off because every choice feels like failing someone, and who could help me weigh it?

weeks.focus: A life that outlasts these years
weeks.why: Caregiving seasons end, sometimes slowly and sometimes all at once, and you can come out the far side to find your own life worn thin: friendships gone quiet, a marriage running on logistics, a faith reduced to emergency prayers. A rule of life is the church's old name for a few chosen practices that hold a life steady over years, and yours should be small enough to keep on the worst week. In the book of Isaiah, the gods of Babylon have to be loaded onto beasts, "a load to the weary animal" (Isaiah 46:1), while the LORD tells his people, "I have made you, and I will carry you; I will sustain you and deliver you" (Isaiah 46:4). Idols must be carried. The living God carries his people, the one growing old and the one wearing out beside them.
weeks.practice: Write on a card the two or three practices from these weeks that actually helped, with when you'll keep them, and keep them each day. Add one thing that belongs to your own life and not to the care: a weekly call with a friend, worship with your church, an evening with your husband or wife. Show the card to one person and ask them to check on you in a month.

read.label: How to Build a Rule of Life, on choosing a few small practices that hold a life steady

tool.label: The Rule of Life Builder, choose a few rhythms you can keep through the caregiving years

weeks.reflection: What part of my own life do I most want still standing when this season ends, and what will I do this week to protect it?
